concepts.def: Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described using four quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength describes how long one complete wave is; frequency and period describe its timing and are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f. Wave speed is a further quantity, but it is calculated from frequency and wavelength rather than being one of the four descriptive quantities.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed line up to a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to a trough — never from a trough all the way up to a crest, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is read on the displacement axis of a wave diagram.

The undisturbed position is where a point in the medium would sit if no wave were passing — its rest position. On a wave diagram it is the centre line about which the wave oscillates, and it is the line from which amplitude is measured. Displacement is measured from this line, so a point at the undisturbed position has zero displacement even though the wave is still passing.

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. Crest to the next crest, trough to the next trough, or any point to the matching point one wave later all give the same distance. Wavelength is given the symbol λ and measured in metres, m. A crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength.

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. It is a counting rate — not a speed, and not a count of how many waves happen to be drawn on a diagram. Frequency is given the symbol f and measured in hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz means one complete wave passing each second.

The period of a wave is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency: period = (1)/(frequency). A high frequency therefore means a short period. A wave of frequency 8 Hz has a period of 1/8 = 0.125 s, because eight waves share each second.

The specification states the relationship as period = (1)/(frequency), in symbols [T = 1/f]. Because the two quantities are reciprocals, the relationship rearranges to f = 1/T, so either can be found from the other. A period of 0.004 s gives f = 1/0.004 = 250 Hz. Period and frequency are never equal in value unless both are 1.

The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s. Period is a time, so its unit is the second — the same unit as any other time interval. Periods of waves are often small fractions of a second, so answers such as 0.004 s are normal and should not be rounded to zero or converted into hertz.

The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz is one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies are often quoted in kilohertz, kHz, or megahertz, MHz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz, so a frequency in kHz is multiplied by 1000 to convert it into hertz before it is used in the wave equation.

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. It is not the speed of the particles of the medium, which only oscillate about their undisturbed positions and are not carried along with the wave. Wave speed is given the symbol v and measured in metres per second, m/s.

concepts.term: All waves obey the wave equation
concepts.def: All waves obey the wave equation: it holds for transverse and longitudinal waves alike, and for waves in air, in fluids and in solids. Sound, ripples on water, waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are all covered by the same relationship, so a single equation links speed, frequency and wavelength for every wave met in this course.

The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength, in symbols [v = f λ]. It rearranges to f = v/λ and to λ = v/f. Because the speed is a product of the other two, a wave that keeps the same speed has a wavelength that falls as its frequency rises. Substituting f in Hz and λ in m always gives v in m/s.

The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; and wavelength, λ, in metres, m. The equation only produces a speed in m/s if the wavelength is entered in metres and the frequency in hertz, so a wavelength quoted in centimetres or millimetres must be converted first, and a frequency in kilohertz must be multiplied by 1000.

concepts.term: Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram
concepts.def: On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or trough, while wavelength is read horizontally on the distance axis, from one point to the equivalent point on the next wave. The two quantities are therefore measured on different axes, and confusing the axes is the commonest error when identifying them from a given diagram.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of sound in air
concepts.def: A workable method is to stand a measured distance from a large reflecting wall, clap, and time the echo returning; the sound has travelled twice the distance to the wall, so wave speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time. Distances of many tens of metres, and timings taken over several claps, are used so that human reaction time is small compared with the time being measured. An alternative method uses two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an electronic timer.

concepts.term: Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface
concepts.def: A ripple tank with a vibrating dipper produces ripples whose pattern is projected onto a screen below. The frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper, and the wavelength is measured with a ruler laid against the projected pattern, ideally across ten wavelengths which are then divided by ten. The wave speed is then found from v = f λ. A stroboscope or a video frame freezes the moving pattern so that it can be measured.

concepts.term: Sound passing from one medium to another
concepts.def: When a sound wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency is fixed by the vibrating source and does not change. The wave speed does change, because it depends on the medium — sound travels faster in water, and faster still in solids, than in air. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: a faster medium gives a longer wavelength.

In this practical, observations are made to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and of waves in a solid, and appropriate measurements are taken. Typical judgements include using a ruler on the projected pattern rather than a stopwatch on a single ripple, reading the frequency from the signal generator, and measuring across ten wavelengths on a stretched string before dividing by ten.

mcqs.q: A transverse wave is drawn with its undisturbed position shown as a horizontal centre line. What is the amplitude of this wave?
options: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
The vertical distance from the bottom of a trough up to the top of a crest
The displacement of a point on the wave at the instant it is measured
The distance a point on the wave travels while one whole wave passes
mcqs.explain: The specification definition: amplitude is measured from the undisturbed line to a crest or trough.

mcqs.q: Which distance on a wave diagram is exactly one wavelength?
options: From the first crest drawn on the diagram to the very last crest drawn
From a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave
From the top of a crest to the bottom of the trough next to it
From the centre line up to the top of the crest above it
mcqs.explain: The specification definition; crest to the next crest is the usual example of it.

mcqs.q: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?
options: The speed at which a wave moves through the medium
The number of complete waves drawn on the diagram
The number of waves passing a point each second
The time taken for one wave to pass a point
mcqs.explain: The specification definition of frequency.

mcqs.q: Which set of four quantities does the specification use to describe wave motion?
options: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and wave speed
Wavelength, frequency, period and wave speed
Amplitude, wavelength, period and wave energy
Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
mcqs.explain: Exactly the four quantities the specification names for describing wave motion.

mcqs.q: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?
options: 8 s
mcqs.explain: period = (1)/(frequency) = 1/8 = 0.125 s.

mcqs.q: A wave has a period of 0.004 s. Using [T = 1/f], what is its frequency?
options: 25 Hz
4 Hz
250 Hz

mcqs.q: Which statement about the period of a wave is correct?
options: It is measured in hertz, the same unit as the frequency
It is measured in waves per second, like the frequency
It is measured in metres, like the wavelength
It is measured in seconds, because it is a time
mcqs.explain: The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s.

mcqs.q: In one second, 400 complete waves pass a point. How should this be recorded?
options: 400 Hz, because 400 waves pass each second
400 s, because the waves are counted over a second
0.0025 Hz, because frequency is one over 400
400 m/s, because the waves move past the point
mcqs.explain: The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz, and 1 Hz is one wave each second.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the wave speed?
options: The speed at which particles of the medium move up and down
The number of complete waves that pass a point each second
The speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium
The speed at which the source producing the wave vibrates
mcqs.explain: The specification defines wave speed as the speed at which the energy is transferred, or the wave moves, through the medium.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the wave equation is correct?
options: It applies only to transverse waves, such as water ripples
It applies to light waves but not to sound waves
It applies only to waves whose speed stays constant
It applies to all waves, transverse and longitudinal
mcqs.explain: The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation.

mcqs.q: How is the wave speed related to the frequency and the wavelength?
options: The wave speed is the frequency times the wavelength
The wave speed is the frequency divided by the wavelength
The wave speed is the frequency added to the wavelength
The wave speed is the amplitude times the frequency
mcqs.explain: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, the equation as the specification states it.

mcqs.q: The wave equation is [v = f λ]. Which rearrangement correctly gives the wavelength?
options: λ = f / v, the frequency divided by the wave speed
λ = v / f, the speed divided by the frequency
λ = v f, the speed multiplied by the frequency
λ = v − f, subtracting the frequency from the speed
mcqs.explain: Dividing both sides of v = f λ by f gives λ = v/f.

mcqs.q: A student uses [v = f λ] with the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres. What unit does the calculated wave speed have?
options: Hertz, Hz, the unit taken from the frequency
Metres, m, the unit taken from the wavelength
Seconds, s, because speed always involves a time
Metres per second, m/s, since the answer is a speed
mcqs.explain: The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.

mcqs.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this frequency in hertz?
options: 250 Hz
25 Hz

mcqs.q: Ripples on a tank have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their wave speed?
options: 2 m/s
2 m

mcqs.q: A wave is shown on a graph of displacement against distance. How are the amplitude and the wavelength read from it?
options: Amplitude runs from a trough up to the crest above it
Both are measured along the horizontal distance axis
Amplitude is vertical, wavelength is horizontal
Wavelength runs from one crest to the next trough
mcqs.explain: Amplitude is read up the displacement axis, wavelength along the distance axis.

mcqs.q: A class measures the speed of sound in air. Which method gives the most reliable value?
options: Time the echo of a clap from a wall a measured distance away
Measure how loud the clap is at two different distances
Use a stopwatch to time a clap crossing the laboratory
Ask two students to clap together and time the delay
mcqs.explain: A long path gives a time large enough for reaction time to matter little; speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time.

mcqs.q: In the echo method for the speed of sound, the distance to the wall is measured but twice that distance is used in the calculation. Why?
options: Because the sound must spread out in every direction from the clap
Because the wall creates a new wave that travels more slowly
Because the sound travels to the wall and back before it is heard
Because sound travels faster on its way back from the wall
mcqs.explain: The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the path is 2 × the distance to the wall.

mcqs.q: Which is a suitable method for measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface?
options: Count the ripples reaching the far edge and multiply by the depth
Use the dipper frequency and a measured wavelength in v = f λ
Measure the height of the ripples and divide it by the frequency
Time one ripple with a stopwatch over a two centimetre gap
mcqs.explain: Frequency is read from the signal generator and wavelength from the projected pattern.

mcqs.q: Why is a stroboscope or a video recording often used when ripples are studied in a ripple tank?
options: It increases the frequency of the ripples on the water surface
It slows the ripples down so they really travel more slowly
It makes the ripples taller so the amplitude can be measured
It freezes the pattern so wavelengths can be measured
mcqs.explain: A still pattern lets a ruler be laid across ten wavelengths on the projected image.

mcqs.q: (Physics only) A sound wave passes from air into water, where it travels faster. What happens to its frequency and its wavelength?
options: The wavelength stays the same and the frequency increases
Both the frequency and the wavelength become larger
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength becomes longer
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength gets shorter
mcqs.explain: With f fixed and v larger, v = f λ requires λ to increase in the same proportion.

mcqs.q: (Physics only) Sound travels faster in a steel rail than in air. When a sound passes from the air into the steel, which quantity is fixed by the source and cannot change?
options: The frequency, which is set by the vibrating source
The wave speed, which depends on the source's energy
The wavelength, because the wave keeps its shape
The period, which grows longer in the steel
mcqs.explain: The source sends the same number of waves each second whatever medium receives them.

mcqs.q: In required practical activity 8, which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank?
options: The frequency dial on the signal generator for the dipper
A ruler measuring the height of a single ripple crest
A stopwatch timing one ripple crossing the tank
A ruler placed under the projected ripple pattern
mcqs.explain: The projected pattern is still enough to measure across, ideally over ten wavelengths.

mcqs.q: In required practical activity 8, waves are also sent along a stretched string. Why is the distance across ten wavelengths measured and then divided by ten?
options: The wavelength changes as the wave crosses the whole string
It reduces the effect of uncertainty in each reading
One wavelength is far too small to be seen on a string
Ten readings must be taken in every school experiment
mcqs.explain: The same ruler uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a ten-times-longer distance.
